elements.content:
• What is HTML and why it matters for web development

• Course objectives and learning outcomes

• Structure of the upcoming lessons

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Ms. Emma Clarke, and I’m excited to welcome you to our Introduction to HTML course. Today we’ll get an overview of what HTML is, why it matters, and what you’ll achieve by the end of this class.

First, let’s talk about the question on the screen: “What is HTML and why it matters for web development?” HTML, or HyperText Markup Language, is the backbone of every webpage—it tells browsers how to structure text, images, links, and more. Without HTML, the web would be just a collection of raw files with no meaning.

Next, look at the three main objectives listed here: we’ll learn the basic tags, understand how to build a simple page, and explore how HTML fits into the larger web development workflow. By the end of the course, you’ll be able to create your own functional web pages from scratch.

Finally, the structure of our upcoming lessons will follow a clear pattern: a brief concept introduction, a hands‑on example, and a short practice activity. Keep that in mind as we move forward, and feel free to ask questions at any point.
That’s our roadmap for today—understanding HTML’s role, our learning goals, and how we’ll proceed. Let’s dive in!

elements.content:
• Doctype declaration <!DOCTYPE html>

• Root <html> with <head> and <body>

• Common <head> tags: <title>, <meta charset="UTF-8">

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let’s dive into the basic structure of an HTML document. This is the foundation for every web page you’ll create.

First, we start with the doctype declaration <!DOCTYPE html> — it tells the browser that this is an HTML5 document. Next comes the root <html> element, which wraps everything else. Inside <html> we have two main sections: the <head> and the <body>.
Within the <head>, you typically place metadata like the <title> tag and <meta> tags for character encoding or viewport settings. The <body> is where all the visible content—text, images, links—goes.
So, to recap: doctype, root <html>, then <head> with title and meta, and finally <body> with the page’s actual content. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• <h1>‑<h6> hierarchy & semantic meaning

• Use <p> for paragraph text

• Write meaningful, descriptive headings

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's dive into headings and paragraphs. This is the foundation for structuring any web page.
First, we have the heading hierarchy from <h1> down to <h6>. Think of it like an outline: <h1> is your main title, and each lower level adds more detail.
Using these tags correctly also gives meaning to screen readers and improves SEO, because they understand the importance of each section.

Next, notice the paragraph element

A quick best‑practice tip: write headings that actually describe the content that follows. That way your page is both readable for people and meaningful for machines.

elements.content:
• Create hyperlinks with <a href="...">

• Embed images using <img src="..." alt="...">

• Use descriptive alt text for accessibility

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let’s dive into today’s topic: Links and Images.
First, creating a hyperlink is as simple as using the <a href="…"> tag. You place the URL inside the href attribute, and the linked text goes between the opening and closing tags.
Next, to embed an image, we use the tag. The src points to the image file, and the alt attribute provides a description for screen readers.
Remember, writing clear, descriptive alt text is crucial for accessibility—it helps users who rely on assistive technology understand what the image shows.
That covers the basics of links and images. Try adding a hyperlink and an image to your own page, and we’ll review your code together.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to create a top-level heading?
questions.analysis: The <h1> tag defines the most important heading. <heading> is not a valid HTML tag, <title> defines the page title in the head section, and <head> is a container for meta-information.

elements.content:
• Ordered lists: <ol> + <li>

• Unordered lists: <ul> + <li>

• Simple tables: <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td>

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into Lists and Tables. We'll see how to create ordered and unordered lists, and then build a simple table.
First, an ordered list uses the <ol> tag together with <li> for each item. This automatically numbers the items for you.
Next, an unordered list uses the <ul> tag with <li> items, giving you bullet points instead of numbers.
Now, let's look at building a simple table. We start with the <table> element, then add rows with <tr>, header cells with <th>, and data cells with <td>.
Great job! Remember, lists help organize information, and tables let you compare data neatly. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Form container <form> with action attribute

• Common inputs: <input>, <textarea>, <button>

• Use <label> to associate text with inputs for accessibility

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into the basics of HTML forms. We'll see how to gather user input and make our pages interactive.
First, every form starts with a <form> container. The action attribute tells the browser where to send the data when the user submits the form.
Next, inside the form we use common input elements like <input> for single‑line data, <textarea> for longer text, and <button> to trigger submission.
Finally, pairing each input with a <label> improves accessibility, letting screen readers and users know exactly what information is required.
That covers the three core pieces: the form container with its action, the basic input elements, and proper labeling for accessibility. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Semantic elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Improves accessibility & SEO

• Clean code: proper indentation, meaningful IDs/classes

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into Semantic HTML and good coding practices. This helps us write pages that are both understandable to browsers and accessible to users.
First, notice the list of semantic elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. These tags describe the purpose of each part of the page, making the structure clear.
Why does that matter? Semantic tags improve accessibility because screen readers can announce sections correctly, and they boost SEO since search engines understand the content hierarchy.
Lastly, clean code formatting—consistent indentation and meaningful IDs or class names—makes our HTML easier to read, maintain, and collaborate on.
To recap, we covered the key semantic elements, their benefits for accessibility and SEO, and the importance of tidy code conventions. Any quick questions before we move on?

questions.question: Which HTML5 semantic element is most appropriate for marking up the main navigation links of a website?
questions.analysis: The <nav> element is specifically designed to contain a set of navigation links. <section> groups related content, <article> represents an independent piece of content, and <aside> holds tangential information.

questions.question: Select all HTML elements that are valid choices for creating a list of items (select all that apply).
questions.analysis: <ul> (unordered list) and <ol> (ordered list) are both list containers. <dl> is a description list, not a generic item list, and <table> is for tabular data.

questions.question: Name three common HTML form controls used to collect user input and briefly describe the type of data each is best suited for.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Mention at least three distinct form controls - 40%, (2) Correctly describe the typical data each collects - 40%, (3) Clarity and completeness of explanation - 20%
questions.analysis: A strong answer might mention: • <input type="text"> for short, free‑form text such as names or email addresses; • <textarea> for longer, multi‑line text like comments; • <select> (with <option> elements) for a predefined list of choices; optionally also <input type="checkbox"> for binary yes/no or multiple selections, and <input type="radio"> for exclusive choice among options.

actions.text: Alright, it's time for our final knowledge check! This short quiz will bring together everything we've learned about semantic tags, list structures, and form controls. Read each question carefully and choose the best answer.

Remember, the <nav> element is designed specifically for navigation links, while <section> groups related content, <article> represents a self‑contained composition, and <aside> holds tangential information. Keep that in mind for the first question.

For lists, think about the purpose: <ul> and <ol> are for unordered and ordered lists of items, <dl> is for definition lists, and a <table> is for tabular data, not typical list items. And when you get to the form controls, recall that <input type="text"> captures short text, <textarea> handles longer multi‑line input, and <select> lets users pick from a set of options.
Good luck! Once you’ve answered, we’ll review the correct responses together and highlight any common pitfalls.
